name: Forum of Trajan
summary: The last and largest of Rome's imperial forums: a vast colonnaded square paid for with the spoils of the Dacian Wars and dedicated in AD 112. A gilded bronze statue of Trajan on horseback stood in the middle of the square.

name: Basilica Ulpia
summary: An enormous columned hall closing the north-west side of the Forum, used for law courts and public business and named after Trajan's family name, Ulpius. It was one of the largest basilicas ever built in Rome.

name: Trajan's Column
summary: A marble column 100 Roman feet (about 30 m) tall, wrapped in a spiral frieze of some 155 scenes telling the story of the two Dacian Wars. It was dedicated in May 113, and after Trajan's death his ashes were placed in a golden urn in its base.

name: Markets of Trajan
summary: A multi-storey complex of shops, halls and offices built into the slope of the Quirinal Hill beside the Forum. The name is modern; besides shops it probably housed offices of the city administration.

name: Baths of Trajan
summary: Huge public baths built over part of Nero's Golden House on the Oppian Hill and opened in June 109. Their plan—a central bathing block inside a large walled park—became the model for later imperial baths such as those of Caracalla and Diocletian.

name: Aqua Traiana
place: From springs near Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum, Rome (pin at the Janiculum)
summary: An aqueduct that brought spring water nearly 60 km from the hills around Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum Hill, supplying the district across the Tiber and driving water mills. It was opened on 24 June 109, two days after the Baths of Trajan.

name: Portus: Trajan's hexagonal harbour
summary: Trajan added a sheltered hexagonal basin—each side about 358 m long, enclosing some 32 hectares—behind Claudius' harbour near the mouth of the Tiber, linked to the river by a canal. It made Portus the main port for the grain ships that fed the city of Rome.

name: Via Traiana
place: Beneventum to Brundisium, southern Italy (pin at Canusium, about halfway)
summary: A new road built at Trajan's own expense from Beneventum to Brundisium, a shorter and easier route across Apulia than the old Via Appia. It ran by way of towns such as Aecae, Canusium, Barium and Egnatia.

name: Arch of Trajan, Benevento
summary: A triumphal arch voted by the Senate in 114 where the Via Traiana left Beneventum. Its carved panels, among the best preserved on any Roman arch, celebrate Trajan's achievements in Rome, Italy and the provinces.

name: Arch of Trajan, Ancona
summary: A tall, slender marble arch on the harbour mole of Ancona, set up by the Senate and people around 115. Its inscription thanks Trajan for making the harbour safer for sailors at his own expense.

name: Harbour of Ancona
summary: Trajan enlarged Ancona's harbour on the Adriatic with a new mole, improving Italy's main crossing point to Dalmatia and the Danube provinces. A harbour scene on Trajan's Column is often identified as Ancona.

name: Trajan's Bridge over the Danube
summary: A bridge more than 1,100 m long, with 20 masonry piers carrying a timber superstructure, built so the army could cross into Dacia for the Second Dacian War. It is often said to have been the longest arch bridge in the world for over a thousand years; stumps of its piers still stand on both banks.

name: Tabula Traiana and the Iron Gates road
place: Iron Gates gorge of the Danube, Serbia
summary: A carved plaque in the cliffs of the Danube gorge records that in AD 100 Trajan's engineers completed a road cut into the rock face, partly carried on a wooden walkway over the river. The plaque was moved higher up the cliff when the Iron Gates dam (1964–1972) raised the river.

name: Alcántara Bridge
summary: A granite bridge of six arches over the river Tagus, about 45 m high, paid for by local towns of Lusitania and dedicated to Trajan. An inscription names its builder, Gaius Julius Lacer, and it still carries traffic today.
latinNote: Its Latin name is not known; Alcántara comes from the Arabic for "the bridge".

name: Tropaeum Traiani
summary: A huge round victory monument, about 40 m across, dedicated to Mars Ultor (Mars the Avenger) in 109 after the Dacian Wars. Its 54 carved panels show Roman soldiers fighting Dacians and their allies; a Roman town of the same name grew up nearby.

name: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa
latin: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa
summary: The first Roman colony and capital of the new province of Dacia, founded for army veterans by the governor Decimus Terentius Scaurianus. It lay about 40 km west of the ruined Dacian royal seat, Sarmizegetusa Regia, whose name it borrowed.

name: Thamugadi (Timgad)
summary: A colony for army veterans founded in AD 100 by the Third Augustan Legion, laid out on a strict chessboard grid near the Aurès mountains. Its well-preserved ruins—streets, forum, theatre and a later arch known as "Trajan's Arch"—make it a classic example of Roman town planning.

name: Via Nova Traiana
place: Province of Arabia: Bostra to Aila (pin at Petra)
summary: A paved road through the new province of Arabia, built under the governor Gaius Claudius Severus and running over 400 km from Bostra in the north to Aila (Aqaba) on the Red Sea. Its milestones say it ran "from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea".

name: Harbour of Centumcellae
summary: A new harbour on the coast north-west of Rome, protected by two curved moles and an artificial island breakwater at its mouth. Pliny the Younger saw it being built while staying at Trajan's villa there and described it in a letter.

name: Trajan's Kiosk, Philae
summary: An elegant open pavilion of 14 columns beside the Temple of Isis, traditionally called Trajan's Kiosk because reliefs inside show Trajan making offerings to Egyptian gods; the building itself may have been begun earlier, perhaps under Augustus. In the 1970s it was moved with the other temples of Philae to Agilkia Island to save it from the waters of the Aswan dams.

name: Italica (Trajan's birthplace)
summary: The Roman town in the province of Baetica where, according to most ancient sources, Trajan was born in AD 53 into a family of Italian settlers; founded in 206 BC, it was the first Roman town in Spain. Under Hadrian, whose family also came from Italica, the town was greatly enlarged and a temple to the deified Trajan, the Traianeum, was built there.
note: Birthplace, not a Trajanic building project.
